name: operating-layer
title: From engineer to organization
brief: Show a delivery-accountable audience how one engineer's accumulated workflows became an operating layer — and why the durable asset is encoded judgement rather than generated code.

audience.title: Delivery principal
audience.cares: Whether this survives a team that did not build it, and what it costs to keep running.

audience.title: Practice lead
audience.cares: Whether the judgement compounds across engagements or evaporates when the engineer moves on.

evidence.ref: the delivery inventory — REPLACE with your own repository, brand and locale counts
the operating layer's own manifest — agents, commands, hooks, skills, tools, folders
the recorded work items and audit events produced as a side effect of delivery
the acceptance criteria file each run is checked against, written before the code exists
demonstrated live in the one-work-item beat

beats.title: A generic assistant made specialized work slower
beats.narration: It knew the language but not the platform. Not the layering conventions, not the serialization rules, not what this client had already decided. So every task became the same four steps, and I was spending more time briefing the assistant than doing the work.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: by hand, because nothing else would

visual.note: The environment varied. The recurring tasks and the corrections did not.

beats.title: The same exact work, over and over
beats.narration: This is the shape of the estate. One shared platform, inheriting brands, and two dozen legacy sites — the variation is real, but the work each variation demands is not new work.

claims.text: The estate is wide enough that no engineer reads all of it carefully in a quarter.

beats.title: Agentic engineering is progressive encoding
beats.narration: Nothing here was a leap. Each layer answers one question that kept being asked, and each was added the week it was needed. Skills encoded the domain; specialists encoded the recurring roles.

steps.label: Tools
steps.detail: what can be observed or changed?

beats.title: The system accreted in response to real failures
beats.narration: None of this was designed up front. Every layer is still here because it solved a delivery problem that came back — and the ones that did not solve anything were removed.

visual.note: Each layer remained because it solved a delivery problem that came back.

beats.title: By July, one engineer had accumulated an operating system
beats.narration: None of this was planned as a system. It is what is left after nine months of encoding the same answers — and it is small enough that a second engineer can read all of it in an afternoon.

claims.text: The operating layer is inspectable in full: every agent, command, hook and skill is a file in the repository.

visual.note: Nothing here is a black box. Every one of them is a file you can open, diff, and delete.

beats.title: Follow one work item, request to release
beats.narration: One ticket, end to end. I am going to stop it twice, and the second stop is where verification disagrees with the builder — which is the whole point of separating them.

claims.text: Success is made executable before any code exists — the acceptance criteria are written first and checked mechanically.
The audit trail is produced as a side effect of delivery, not assembled afterwards.

live.repo: REPLACE ME — the real delivery repository, not a scratch one
live.task: Read the queue, turn the top ticket into an explicit plan, build only after the plan is inspectable, then verify independently of the builder.
live.fallback: A recorded pass of this exact ticket, cued to the plan step, with the branch already pushed so the verification section still works.
checkpoints: Approve the plan before any file is written.
Read the acceptance criteria together, before the build starts.
Decide as a room whether the verifier's objection blocks the release.
live.expectedFailure: The verifier rejects the first build on an edge case the plan did not cover. Let it fail on stage, read the objection out loud, and amend the plan rather than the verdict.
traceSurfaces: the queue, and which ticket was chosen
the plan, before any file is written
the verifier's verdict, including the rejection

beats.title: Verification must be independent of the builder
beats.narration: Three roles, deliberately separated. The one that builds does not get to decide whether it worked — and a verdict without test output is not a verdict.

columns.heading: Verifier
points: Is the diff scoped to the plan?

columns.heading: QA expert
points: Does it satisfy the acceptance criteria?

visual.note: PASS is not a feeling. A verdict without test output remains unproven.

beats.title: The valuable loop is not generation
beats.narration: Generation is replaceable and getting cheaper every month. What compounds is the encoded judgement — the lessons, the constraints, the things this team decided once and never has to decide again.

claims.text: Every run leaves behind lessons the next run reads on the way in.

beats.title: The goal is not more agents
beats.narration: It is reusable judgement, with accountable humans still deciding the things that carry consequence.

beats.title: Start with one repeated workflow
beats.narration: Do not try to build the operating layer. Pick the one workflow your team repeats every week, encode the context it keeps needing, and make its verification mechanical. Then do the next one.

takeaway: The plan and acceptance-criteria templates, the three verification roles, and the evidence layout used in this demo — enough to encode one repeated workflow of your own this week.
